steps.action: Pose the question of whether backazimuthal variation of SK(K)S splitting reflects layered, laterally homogeneous anisotropy or lateral variation, given limited azimuthal coverage and averaging practice.
steps.quote: Another problem is the assumption of laterally uniform structural anisotropy around a recording station

steps.action: Take the published BFO anisotropy models as starting rivals: Vinnik's averaged one-layer value, Walker's dipping one-layer or two two-layer options, and Walther's two-layer model.
steps.quote: propose two options for BFO: either one-layer with transverse isotropy with dipping symmetry axis

steps.action: Select SK(K)S recordings from 25 years of continuous low-noise BFO data (1166 events, Mw≥6, 90–130°), leaving 318 events after visual inspection.
steps.quote: We analyzed 25 years of continuously recorded data (July 1991 – October 2016) from BFO.

steps.action: Check the relative temporal alignment of the N, E, Z traces against a known SplitLab error that can produce wrong splitting measurements.
steps.quote: We checked the relative temporal alignment of the single traces (N, E, Z components) regarding an error source in SplitLab.

steps.action: Measure single-event splitting parameters with the RC and SC methods after bandpass filtering and manual windowing, apply Walsh et al. error estimation, assign quality classes, and classify nulls.
steps.quote: using two different and independent approaches: the rotation-correlation method

steps.action: Cross-check each measurement by requiring agreement of RC and SC within 95% confidence and SNR ≥ 7.
steps.quote: we report only results for which the SC and the RC methods agree within their error bounds

steps.action: Stabilize poor measurements with SIMW multi-event inversion and stack single-event measurements in 5° backazimuth bins, giving 77 splits and 241 nulls in total.
steps.quote: we applied the simultaneous inversion of multiple waveforms (SIMW) method

steps.action: Split the record into five-year periods and show that each subset is too short and that averaging a subset would give a wrong one-layer model.
steps.quote: such an observational period is too short to achieve a representative result even for a low-noise recording site such as BFO

steps.action: Establish two features in the 25-year dataset: nulls dominating about three-quarters of the backazimuth range, and a short-scale flip of the fast axis in the NE quadrant.
steps.quote: nearly three-quarters of the BAZ range are dominated by nulls

steps.action: Show that splitting parameters repeat for different events from the same source region, and that SKS and SKKS agree.
steps.quote: are clearly aligned for measurements from the same source region

steps.action: Exclude a lowermost-mantle origin of the splitting because SKS and SKKS from the same source give the same parameters, and place the anisotropy in the upper mantle.
steps.quote: do not seem to play a major role along the different ray paths of these two phases

steps.action: State the rival structural models for the NE quadrant: one-layer and two-layer transverse isotropy with horizontal symmetry axes; models with more than two layers or dipping layers are ruled out as unconstrained.
steps.quote: We limit the tested models to one-layer and two-layer cases with transverse isotropy

steps.action: Compute the predicted backazimuthal splitting patterns with the Silver and Savage equations in MSAT, and cite the expected slopes and jumps of ϕ near null directions.
steps.quote: The forward modeling or calculation is done based on the equations by Silver and Savage

steps.action: Design the test: SC non-null measurements only, NE quadrant 30–100°, grid search in 5° and 0.25 s steps, normalized joint RMSE, and the 20 best-fit models examined.
steps.quote: a systematic sampling of the model space is done with 5° steps for the fast polarization direction

steps.action: Fit all good and fair measurements: the one-layer best fit is 35° and 1.25 s (RMSE 0.47); two-layer fits reach RMSE about 0.46 but fit ϕ poorly.
steps.quote: It is obvious that no theoretical curve for two-layer models fits very well the distributions of the measurements.

steps.action: Compare the one-layer prediction with the observed nulls: no nulls are found at the modeled 35° direction, while nulls lie between 55° and 75°.
steps.quote: there are no observed nulls in the modeled fast polarization direction 35° as expected from theory

steps.action: Refit one- and two-layer models to the 5° binned dataset to remove the over-representation of the 60–90° backazimuths.
steps.quote: To avoid an over-representation of specific BAZ directions in the NE quadrant, we stacked the splitting parameters in 5° bins.

steps.action: Reject the one-layer model (RMSE 0.51) in favour of the two-layer model (RMSE 0.36, about 30% lower), which matches the backazimuthal variation of ϕ and δt.
steps.quote: The one-layer models are not appropriate to fit the measurements

steps.action: Compare the null positions and the π/2 jump in ϕ with the two-layer theory and with Eakin et al.'s one-layer synthetic jump; the data match the two-layer case better.
steps.quote: It better coincides with the change in ϕ given in Silver and Savage

steps.action: Examine the spread of the 20 best-fit two-layer models: parameters scatter widely for nearly equal RMSE.
steps.quote: the model parameter distribution of the 20 best-fit models in Fig. 8c has a quite large scatter

steps.action: Compare the best-fit two-layer prediction around all backazimuths with the null-dominated observations outside the NE quadrant, indicating lateral variation of anisotropy.
steps.quote: do not fit to the prediction for the gray backazimuthal range, indicating a lateral variation of the anisotropy

steps.action: Re-inspect the null waveforms to confirm that the T-component signal is missing for well-observed Q-component arrivals.
steps.quote: we carefully looked at the waveforms to confirm the missing signal on the T component

steps.action: List rival explanations of the null anomaly: orthogonal cancelling layers, other simple TI models, vertical fast axis or C-type olivine fabric, weak anisotropy, isotropy, scattering, and lowermost-mantle effects.
steps.quote: which we tentatively call the null anomaly

steps.action: Argue against several rivals: simple horizontal and dipping TI models, weak anisotropy (given high-SNR nulls), pristine isotropy, and lowermost-mantle anisotropy (given SKS/SKKS agreement); others remain open.
steps.quote: An influence of anisotropy and splitting effects from the lowermost mantle cannot explain the null anomaly at BFO.

steps.action: Keep the claims that the NE flip is best explained by a two-layer model, that anisotropy varies laterally at small scale, and that averaging is misleading; leave the null anomaly unexplained.
steps.quote: This flip is currently explained best with a two-layer model

end.claim: Upper mantle anisotropy below BFO varies laterally on short scales: the NE-quadrant flip is best explained by a two-layer model (upper ϕ2=40°, lower ϕ1=−60°) that fails for the null-dominated other quadrants, so backazimuthal averaging is misleading.

decisive_move.sentence: Comparing the best-fit NE two-layer prediction with the null-dominated observations at other backazimuths is what turns a station model into the claim of lateral variation.

gates.evidence: Data were all archived BFO events selected by magnitude and distance, not directed by a hypothesis (§3 ¶1). The one-layer model could fail and did (§5.1 ¶1, §5.2 ¶2). The two-layer model was the best of two rivals on the same data, with no held-out test (§5.2 ¶2–¶3). The lateral-variation claim rests on a mismatch with nulls (Fig. 9). Grid steps and RMSE were set in the Methods, but nothing is stated as fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: birefringence as analogue for shear wave splitting

novelty_claims.quote: Here, we analyze an exceptional dataset from the permanent broadband seismological recording station Black Forest Observatory (BFO)
Our 77 plus 241 observations are much more than reported in other studies.
small-scale laterally varying anisotropy may play a more important role in the study region than previously thought

limits: Sub-claims and their statuses: two-layer parameters are an estimate_with_resolution with large scatter (±10–20° for ϕ, ±0.5 s for δt; §6 ¶2); the null anomaly has no conclusion, and the rivals (c) vertical fast axis or C-type fabric and (f) scattering remain open (§5.3 ¶11); the upper-mantle location of the anisotropy rests on SKS/SKKS agreement (best_explanation). The paper does not report how many waveforms the visual and manual selection rejected beyond 1166 to 318 events, so selection effects cannot be assessed. Nulls were excluded from the quantitative fit and compared only qualitatively. The lateral-variation claim is inferred from misfit, not from a laterally varying model fitted to the data. The supplement (Figs. S1–S4) was not supplied, so the steps citing it are taken from the main text. No review file was supplied, though the acknowledgements thank two referees; changes made in review are unknown. Composition is coded trace_series by inference: sources are natural earthquakes, found rather than set, repeated over 25 years; strictly these are recorded live events, not traces, so natures_repetition or none_fits are defensible alternatives.

disagreements.target: Backazimuthal averaging of splitting parameters for laterally homogeneous models, as mainly done in the past (e.g., Vinnik et al. 1994)
disagreements.support: The observed backazimuthal variations, the near-perpendicular ϕ pairs in the 1992–1996 subset, and the NE flip show that averaging yields a meaningless fast direction.
disagreements.quote: do clearly not allow a backazimuthal averaging of the splitting parameters of all (good and fair) splitting measurements

disagreements.support: Null splits over 155–335° backazimuth are not predicted by the published one- or two-layer models for the region.
disagreements.quote: This null anomaly cannot be explained satisfactorily yet and is partly different to published regional anisotropy models.

disagreements.target: Eakin et al. (2019) synthetic one-layer jump in ϕ for the SC method
disagreements.support: The observed jump of about π/2 is larger than the one-layer artifact and matches the two-layer prediction of Silver and Savage (1994).
disagreements.quote: appears to be larger than the synthetic error or jump for a one-layer anisotropy model proposed by Eakin et al.

disagreements.target: Lynner and Long (2012) lowermost-mantle explanation of a similar split/null pattern at DBIC
disagreements.support: At BFO, SKS and SKKS show no discrepancies, so lowermost-mantle anisotropy cannot account for the nulls.
disagreements.quote: An influence of anisotropy and splitting effects from the lowermost mantle cannot explain the null anomaly at BFO.

disagreements.target: Assumption of laterally uniform anisotropy around a station
disagreements.support: The best-fit NE two-layer model fails to predict the null-dominated other quadrants.
disagreements.quote: Thus, small-scale laterally varying anisotropy may play a more important role in the study region than previously thought.
